objectives: Secure UK acceptance of the Article XXVIII modification without triggering a WTO dispute or withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions

Preserve the 50% out-of-quota rate and the core architecture of the TRQ (global first-come-first-served baseline) as far as possible, treating any country-specific carve-out as a costly concession, not a starting point
Prevent the UK from aligning with Japan/Korea in a joint FTA-related retaliation or dispute against the EU
Keep any compensation package narrow, quantifiable and contained to steel-adjacent lines rather than opening broader EU schedule concessions
Maintain a workable long-term relationship with the UK Geneva team across other goods files, since this is a repeated game
Avoid setting a precedent that other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) can point to for more generous treatment in their parallel claims

If a UK-specific accommodation is ultimately needed, prefer mechanisms tied to actual trade flow/product mix (e.g., a UK-specific quota share or product carve-out on narrow lines) over volume increases or rate reductions, since these are easier to defend as 'substantially equivalent' and less costly to the broader regime
Get clarity on the UK's own steel safeguard treatment of EU exporters and use reciprocity there as leverage/trade against EU concessions here
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: UK accepts terms recognisably close to the EU's original notification (50% out-of-quota, ~400,000t global TRQ) with at most a modest, well-defined adjustment (e.g. a UK-specific share, a review clause, or narrow product carve-outs) — settled within the four rounds, no retaliation announced, no joint action with Japan/Korea, and the Council can proceed on schedule in June. Partial success: no settlement, EU proceeds with original measure, UK reserves right to withdraw concessions but does so narrowly and without Japan/Korea coalition, and the relationship with UK Geneva counterpart remains workable for future files. Failure: EU forced into large, precedent-setting concessions (large volume increase, EU-wide rate cut, or UK-specific quota far above its 'fair share') to buy UK sign-off; or no settlement AND UK joins a broader coalition with Japan/Korea that escalates into a wider dispute or cross-retaliation affecting EU exports; or the process drags past June and disrupts the Council's schedule.
declaration.approach: Open firm: restate the EU's systemic rationale (non-market economy overcapacity, permanent legal footing) and treat the original notification as the anchor, not a mere opening bid. Do not offer movement in Round 1 — invite the UK to articulate its position and quantify the harm precisely, so any later concession is clearly a response to demonstrated injury rather than a default expectation. Use Phase 2 consultations to calibrate: only recommend movement to Brussels once we see whether the UK's ask is narrow (product lines, quota share, review clause) or broad (volume/rate). Signal willingness to discuss UK-specific quota share and a review clause as the most likely landing zone, since these are targeted and defensible as 'substantially equivalent,' but resist being drawn into raising the global TRQ volume or lowering the 50% rate, as these ripple into Turkey/Korea's claims and into the Council's political tolerance. Use the FTA-disapplication provision as a bargaining chip — a UK carve-out here (e.g. preserving TCA treatment or a bilateral quota) may be exactly the 'compensation' that lets the UK claim a win without costing us on the headline rate/volume. Keep a close eye on the Japan/Korea dynamic: signal to the UK, informally, that a cooperative bilateral settlement protects UK-specific interests better than a multilateral coalition would, and that the EU is not seeking to link the UK's own safeguard/TRQ process to this one but notes it as context. Escalate to Brussels only with clear asks; avoid revealing flexibility at the table itself. Preserve personal working relationship with UK counterpart regardless of outcome, since we'll face each other on other files.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A UK-specific quota share or carve-out that protects a meaningful volume of tariff-free access to the EU market (their primary export destination), preservation of TCA/FTA-equivalent treatment so they aren't treated worse than other FTA partners, a review clause given the political salience of steel employment, and leverage over EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own safeguard measure. They also want to avoid being seen at home as having accepted a bad deal, so will want a tangible, presentable concession even if modest.

To use the EU's FTA-disapplication move as a wedge to build a coalition with the UK challenging the EU's approach, protecting their own principal-supplier claims and possibly securing joint leverage or precedent for more generous treatment in their own parallel Article XXVIII processes.

To preserve or expand its larger volume share under any TRQ allocation, resisting any UK-specific carve-out that would come at the expense of the global quota pool, and to ensure whatever is agreed with the UK doesn't set a precedent that shortchanges its own (larger) claim.

parties.who: Brussels (Council / Member States via Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A settlement or successful completion of the process in time for the June Council vote, minimal erosion of the headline 50%/400,000t architecture, protection for EU steel-producing member states' interests, but also awareness from steel-consuming member states not to let the measure become needlessly punitive or legally exposed to retaliation.

objectives: Secure a UK settlement within four rounds that preserves the core architecture of the EU regime: a 50% out-of-quota bound rate and a TRQ well below current trade volumes, without opening the door to a broad country-specific carve-out that other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) would then demand parity on.
Obtain a UK-specific quota share (if any) that is meaningfully below the UK's historic 2.4Mt/year average, framed as compensation rather than as a precedent-setting country allocation.
Preserve Commission and member-state political cover: keep the deal defensible to steel-producing member states as a genuine tightening of import access, not a rollback.
Avoid a no-deal outcome that pushes the vote past June, while not paying for that timing pressure with excessive concessions if it can be avoided.
Protect the disapplication of FTA-preferential steel access as leverage/compensation currency, trading it selectively rather than abandoning it outright.
Keep the FTA preferential pool ambiguous/small to avoid the US and others demanding similar treatment, and avoid triggering escalation with the US over retaliation on unrelated grounds.
If settlement fails, ensure the UK's likely retaliation is anticipated and its scale is proportionate/manageable for EU exporters.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a signed agreement within four rounds giving the UK a bounded, clearly-capped volume of tariff-free access (materially below 2.4Mt), a 50% out-of-quota rate intact, no open-ended review clause that could be used to relitigate volumes upward, and language on FTA disapplication that gives us flexibility without a fight now. Failure looks like: conceding a UK-specific quota at or near historic trade levels, agreeing a review clause with automatic escalation, abandoning the 50% rate, or triggering a no-deal collapse that both delays the Council vote past June AND invites UK retaliation on EU exporters (3.6Mt) that member states will blame on DG TRADE's handling.
declaration.approach: Open firm: reaffirm the original notified terms as the baseline and make clear that volume increases must be earned through compensation elsewhere in the schedule, not simply granted because the UK is a principal supplier. Use the fact that no-deal hurts the UK more than the EU as backbone for patience — do not move early. Let the UK articulate its asks first at the table each round; treat any early flexibility from me as costly, so hold position through round 1-2, then in round 3 offer a modest, carefully bounded concession (e.g., a UK-specific slice of the global quota, or a slightly larger overall TRQ) framed as final and linked to something we get in return (e.g., UK flexibility on FTA disapplication, or on the UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters). Keep the country-specific allocation question deliberately ambiguous as long as possible to avoid setting a precedent Turkey/Korea will invoke. Use the June deadline pressure symmetrically — remind the UK team that delay damages them more, without overplaying it to the point of no return.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A UK-specific quota share close to their historic 2.4Mt export volume, a lower or zero out-of-quota rate on at least core product lines, protection or reciprocal treatment under the EU-UK TCA, and a review clause to allow renegotiation if the TRQ proves too restrictive. They will also want reassurance on treatment of EU exporters under their own safeguard as a linked deliverable, and will be under real pressure given concentrated employment impacts.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via TPC)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tightening of import access, suspicion of any UK-specific carve-out that dilutes the global TRQ's restrictiveness, and insistence that the 50% rate and overall volume cap are not diluted just to close the file quickly.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Enough tariff-free volume (including realistic UK access) to avoid input cost shocks; pressure on the Commission not to be too rigid and to conclude on time.

To watch the UK settlement closely as a precedent; will demand equivalent or better treatment on volumes/allocation method if the UK gets a favourable country-specific share, since Turkey and Korea have larger volumes at stake.

To use the EU's Article XXVIII process as a pretext or trigger for its own retaliatory tariff threats, independent of the UK negotiation's content, adding urgency to closing this file quickly and cleanly.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK TRQ share (not global first-come-first-served) reflecting historical trade volumes (~2.4mt), to give certainty rather than a race with Turkey/Korea

Preserve tariff-free access for the bulk of current UK export volume, either via a carve-out on the most exposed product lines (HRC, plate, rebar, wire rod mix specific to UK) or a materially larger quota volume than the EU's 400,000t global figure
Prevent disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel specifically — resist being treated worse than other FTA partners given the TCA relationship
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration, not an open-ended permanent measure, to allow revisiting as global overcapacity conditions change
Protect UK leverage in its own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process — avoid giving away EU exporters' quota treatment cheaply as unilateral compensation
Avoid escalation into joint retaliation with Japan/Korea unless UK interests clearly served — keep UK's dispute independent and controllable
If no deal, ensure UK is positioned to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions credibly and with capital's full backing, not drift into no-deal by default
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share close to historical trade volumes, tariff-free or low out-of-quota rate on the product lines that matter most to UK producers, no discriminatory disapplication of TCA treatment, and a review/duration clause — achieved without London having had to make unreciprocated concessions on the UK's own steel measure. Partial success: a country share and some carve-outs but reduced volumes, offset by real compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule. Failure: settling for something close to the EU's opening offer (global FCFS 400k tonnes, 50% out-of-quota, FTA disapplication, no review), or no deal at all with the UK unprepared to retaliate effectively, leaving the steel industry to absorb an uncushioned shock.
declaration.approach: Hold a firm opening position and do not signal flexibility in Round 1 — the EU is under time pressure (June Council vote) and I am not. Use that asymmetry: they need a deal faster than I do. Press first on facts and process — establish clearly on record that the UK is a principal supplying interest and that the current offer is not compensation but a near-total exclusion, which is not consistent with 'substantially equivalent' treatment. Ask hard, specific questions to establish what the EU can actually move on (volume, country allocation, FTA disapplication, review clause) before revealing any UK ask in detail. Avoid naming a settlement figure until I understand their real constraints and have capital guidance. Keep the UK's own steel measure and Turkey/Korea/Japan dynamics off the table as leverage to be used deliberately, not given away in conversation. Treat the Japan/Korea retaliation approach with caution — useful pressure but risks losing control of UK's bespoke position and tying UK hands; keep them at arm's length while gathering what they know of the EU's flexibility.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, low-cost settlement that lets Council vote in June; wants to protect the 50%/400kt global architecture as the domestic-legislation baseline; will resist country-specific carve-outs because of precedent for Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims; may offer minor compensation on unrelated lines rather than volume/allocation concessions; wants to keep FTA disapplication as leverage against UK's own TCA-related asks.

Protection of UK steel jobs and production sites concentrated in a few constituencies; low tolerance for a deal seen as capitulation; will want visible wins (volume, product carve-outs, TCA protection) before clearing any settlement; may be cautious about triggering retaliation that harms UK manufacturing consumers of EU steel inputs.

To recruit the UK into joint FTA retaliation to increase pressure on the EU on the FTA-disapplication point specifically, serving their own larger-volume claims; want UK's diplomatic and legal weight without necessarily aligning with UK's narrower product-line interest.
Pursuing their own larger-volume claims separately; not directly engaged with UK but their outcomes will set precedent/comparators the EU will cite to resist UK-specific treatment.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Push Commission to hold firm on high protection (50% rate, tight quota) domestically.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Push Commission for more generous quota volumes and continued low-cost input access, potentially a source of internal EU flexibility I can probe for.

objectives: Secure a UK-specific country share of the TRQ (not pure global first-come-first-served) sufficient to broadly preserve recent trade volumes, ideally close to or above the 2.4mt average annual UK exports to the EU
Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel, or secure a UK carve-out from that disapplication given the special EU-UK relationship under the TCA
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure is not a permanent one-way ratchet, with a mechanism to revisit volumes/shares
Seek carve-outs or preferential quota treatment on the specific product lines where UK production is concentrated (narrower product range, higher exposure)
Extract EU commitments on enforcement/circumvention provisions that don't disadvantage UK-origin steel relative to other sources
Preserve UK leverage over EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK's own safeguard as a bargaining chip, not a giveaway
Avoid conceding UK safeguard quota improvements for the EU except against real, substantial EU concessions on the TRQ terms above
Avoid being seen to settle for terms worse than the counterfactual (EU proceeding unilaterally) once UK withdrawal rights and any domestic subsidy support are factored in
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK country-specific share of the TRQ materially better than a pure global pool would deliver, no blanket disapplication of TCA preferences for UK steel (or a narrow, time-limited version with review), a review/duration clause, and carve-outs on key product lines — achieved without giving away more on the UK's own safeguard than the EU's concessions justify. This would let ministers credibly tell the steel industry that access has been defended and give the two at-risk plants a real basis to invest. Failure: settling for global FCFS access with no UK share, losing TCA preference entirely, no review clause, and/or trading away UK safeguard allocations cheaply — or conversely, walking away with no deal when a genuinely better outcome was available, forcing reliance on slow, uncertain WTO withdrawal rights and costly domestic subsidy as the only recourse.
declaration.approach: Hold a firm opening position and do not signal flexibility in Round 1 — test whether the EU's proposal is truly fixed or an opening bid, given they've said the domestic legislation itself is still open and shaped by this process. Anchor on the argument that the UK is a principal supplying interest with concentrated, employment-critical production, and that the proposed measure is disproportionate compensation-wise given zero current bound rates. Use the parallel UK safeguard process as leverage: signal (without conceding early) that improved EU allocations there are available, but only late and only against real EU movement on TRQ share, TCA treatment, and review clause. Avoid revealing the subsidy fallback or the two-plants information, as that would undercut UK bargaining position. Escalate concessions only round by round, in response to matched EU movement, consistent with the belief that early flexibility invites further demands. Keep ministers informed each round and secure clearance before any final acceptance.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To lock in a durable, high legal-certainty steel regime addressing overcapacity from non-market economies, ideally with a global TRQ that limits political fights over country shares internally among member states, while managing pressure from steel-producing member states (protection) versus steel-consuming member states (access), and wanting to conclude by June for Council sign-off.

Maximum preserved tariff-free access to the EU market, ideally a guaranteed country-specific quota, protection from FTA-driven trade diversion, and enough certainty/duration to justify continued investment in the two at-risk plants.
Continued open access to EU steel inputs (i.e., not wanting UK to retaliate in ways that raise their input costs), and are likely to lobby against aggressive UK withdrawal of concessions on EU steel.
A politically defensible outcome that visibly protects steel jobs and plants, without having to immediately deploy costly subsidy; want to be seen as tough but successful negotiators.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, Japan, India (other principal suppliers/substantial interests)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own adequate country shares or safeguards in the EU TRQ; largely irrelevant to direct UK-EU bargaining but their larger volumes may shape how much room is left in the global TRQ envelope for the UK.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g., via Council/Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Tight quotas and high protection, resisting generous country-specific carve-outs for the UK.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming industries
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: More liberal TRQ terms and continued affordable access to UK steel, potentially allies for a UK-friendly outcome.

public_message: Thank you for joining. As you know, the EU has notified under Article XXVIII its intention to modify bound rates on 41 steel tariff lines, moving to a 50% bound rate with a global TRQ of 400,000 tonnes at zero duty, administered first-come first-served, and disapplying FTA-preferential rates for non-EEA partners on these lines. That is the notified position and remains our starting point. We recognise the UK's principal supplying interest under Article XXVIII and we are here in good faith to hear your position on volumes, allocation and compensation before either side fixes anything further. We are not proposing a UK-specific carve-out at this stage, but we are willing to listen to your case for one, and to discuss duration, review mechanisms and enforcement provisions as part of a package. We would find it useful to hear, concretely, what the UK considers would constitute substantially equivalent compensation, and what allocation method you believe reflects your trade share, before we respond in detail.

other_terms: FTA tariff reductions disapplied for non-EEA partners, including the UK, remains on the table as notified
EU open to discussing enforcement/circumvention provisions
EU open to hearing UK proposals on country-specific allocation and compensation elsewhere in the schedule, but has not agreed to either

expectations.what_you_expect_next: UK will assert its principal supplying interest, likely request a country-specific tranche within the pool and object to FTA disapplication
expectations.why: UK's £3bn/2.4mt trade share and concentrated product exposure give it strong grounds to press for a dedicated share rather than compete in a global first-come first-served pool

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation to hold the notified position as anchor and not move on figures until UK tables its own numbers
expectations.why: Consistent with instruction that flexibility offered early invites further demands; need UK's concrete ask before conceding ground

private_rationale: Opening firm at the notified position preserves maximum negotiating room and tests the UK's actual demands before the EU reveals any willingness to carve out a UK-specific tranche or move on the out-of-quota rate. Signalling openness to 'listen' on allocation and compensation keeps the process looking good-faith (important for Article XXVIII optics and for discouraging a UK-Japan-Korea joint retaliation coalition) without committing to any number. Holding the line on FTA disapplication for now avoids signalling early that this is a soft point, since it's likely to be one of the more valuable concessions to trade away later in exchange for the UK dropping retaliation threats or joining Japan/Korea.

public_message: Thank you. To be clear at the outset: the UK does not accept that a global, first-come first-served TRQ of 400,000 tonnes is a reasonable basis for discussion. That volume represents roughly one-sixth of our current trade on these lines, allocated in a manner that structurally disadvantages a supplier with our product concentration against larger-volume shippers. Nor do we accept the disapplication of TCA preference for UK-origin steel — the UK is not a third country in the sense your FTA carve-out is aimed at; we have a bilateral agreement with the EU specifically covering this trade, and unpicking it inside an Article XXVIII process aimed at non-market-economy overcapacity is not proportionate and is not something we will treat as a minor drafting matter. Our starting position is a country-specific tranche reflecting our historic trade share — in the region of our recent annual average — administered by licence rather than first-come first-served, with the TCA preferential arrangements preserved in full. We would expect a genuinely low out-of-quota rate on any volume above that tranche, a short duration with a mandatory review clause, and enforcement language on transhipment that doesn't function as a backdoor restriction on UK-origin product. We are ready to discuss compensation elsewhere in your schedule, but only once we have clarity that the core TRQ design does not simply pre-determine the outcome against us. We'd like to hear how the Commission proposes to reflect principal supplying interest in the allocation method, not just in the consultation process.

other_terms: TCA tariff preference for UK-origin steel preserved in full; no disapplication of FTA rates for UK
Quota administered by licence, not first-come first-served
Enforcement/circumvention provisions targeted at non-market-economy transhipment, not UK-origin product
Compensation on other EU schedule lines to be discussed once TRQ design is settled

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that likely stays close to their notified position on total pool size but may move on allocation method (country-specific vs global) and signal openness on duration/review, while resisting the TCA point strongly given member state sensitivities
expectations.why: The Commission has a tight mandate and Council timeline; they will want to appear responsive on process (licensing, review) before conceding on volume, and the FTA disapplication is likely tied to broader anti-circumvention policy they won't drop lightly at round 1

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Endorsement of firm opening line and the TCA red line; guidance on whether a country-specific tranche below 2.4Mt is acceptable as a landing zone, and steer on compensation appetite
expectations.why: I have not been given a settlement figure; need capital's tolerance for trade-offs between tranche size, out-of-quota rate, and compensation before I move further

private_rationale: Opening firm and high is consistent with the instruction that flexibility offered early invites further demands, and London has said the EU's opening is far from acceptable. Anchoring on our historic volume as the tranche size gives room to concede in later rounds while holding the TCA disapplication as a genuine red line, since that touches a different, larger negotiation (the TCA itself) and conceding it here would set a bad precedent independent of the steel volumes. Proposing licensing over FCFS also protects UK exporters against being outcompeted procedurally by Turkey/Korea's larger volumes. I've avoided committing to any specific compensation offer or reacting to the Japan/Korea approach at the table — that's a separate track for capital to weigh, not something to signal here where the EU can see it.

report: First substantive session. We restated the notified position in full (50% bound rate, 400,000t global TRQ, FCFS, FTA disapplication for non-EEA partners) as our starting point and invited the UK to set out its concrete ask before we moved further. The UK rejected the global/FCFS design outright as structurally disadvantageous given their concentrated product mix relative to higher-volume shippers (they clearly mean Turkey/Korea). They also rejected FTA/TCA disapplication as disproportionate, arguing the TCA is a bilateral instrument distinct from the NME-overcapacity rationale for the measure. Their opening ask: a country-specific tranche pegged to their historic ~2.4Mt average, licensed administration rather than FCFS, TCA preference preserved in full, a low out-of-quota rate, short duration with mandatory review, and anti-circumvention language they say must not function as a de facto restriction on UK-origin product. They conditioned discussion of compensation on getting clarity that the TRQ design itself won't pre-determine the outcome against them. No concessions were made or implied by us; we kept the floor on allocation methodology deliberately unanswered pending capital's steer.

recommendation.reasoning: It is round 1 of 4; the UK has only stated an opening position and has not yet engaged on compensation. We should not move off the notified terms yet — doing so now would confirm to them (and to Turkey/Korea/Japan watching this precedent) that firmness produces early concessions. We should use round 2 to probe whether their 'country-specific tranche at historic share' demand is a genuine red line or an opening bid, and to separate the TRQ-design fight from the TCA-disapplication fight, since conceding on TCA disapplication risks a wider precedent with Japan/Korea who are pushing the UK toward a joint FTA response. We can afford to explore a review clause and duration limits early as low-cost signals of good faith without touching volume, allocation or FTA treatment yet.

instruction: Hold the notified position on volume, allocation method and FTA/TCA disapplication in round 2 — do not concede any of these yet. Do not confirm or deny a floor share; if pressed on 'principal supplying interest', say the Commission is assessing shares against Turkey and Korea and that a global FCFS pool does not preclude UK access commensurate with its trade, since it can draw against the same pool as any other supplier. Decline to engage on a country-specific tranche or licensing at this stage — say the Commission's institutional preference remains global administration for legal-certainty and non-discrimination reasons, but note this is not the only matter on the table. On the TCA/FTA disapplication, do not offer a carve-out, but you may say the Commission is examining whether enforcement/anti-circumvention drafting could address UK concerns about a 'backdoor restriction' without exempting the UK from the general disapplication — frame this as a technical, not substantive, concession. You may table, as the EU's own initiative (not a response to UK demand), a short duration (e.g. 3 years) with a mandatory review clause, presented as reflecting the EU's own confidence that the NME overcapacity problem may evolve, not as a concession to UK pressure. Use this to ask the UK directly what compensation it is prepared to offer elsewhere in the EU schedule, and to press them on whether their 'historic average' ask is genuinely their fallback position or an opening bid — get more specificity from them before we move further. Do not disclose EU import data breakdowns yet. Keep tone firm but constructive; make clear the EU wants a deal in this process but will not pre-concede structure before seeing the UK's compensation offer.

authority.notes: Colleague may float a 3-year duration with mandatory review clause as an EU-initiated, low-cost good-faith gesture, framed as unrelated to UK's specific demand. No movement on volume, allocation method, or FTA/TCA disapplication this round. Colleague may signal that enforcement/anti-circumvention drafting is open for discussion as a technical fix to UK's transhipment concern, without conceding UK-specific carve-out from FTA disapplication. Do not disclose internal floor figures or EU trade-share data. Push UK to specify a concrete compensation offer before any further EU movement.

report: First round held. EU restated its notified position in full: 50% bound rate, 400,000t global TRQ, first-come first-served, FTA/TCA preference disapplied for all non-EEA partners including us. They did not move off any element, but signalled openness to discuss duration, review clauses, enforcement, and possibly a carve-out 'if we make the case'. They explicitly asked us to set out what we'd regard as substantially equivalent compensation and our preferred allocation method before they respond further — classic move to get us to anchor first and negotiate against ourselves. I declined to name a compensation figure. I set out our opening position clearly and firmly: reject global FCFS TRQ at that volume as structurally disadvantageous to a concentrated-product supplier; reject TCA disapplication outright as disproportionate given we're a bilateral partner, not the non-market-economy problem this measure is aimed at; asked for a country-specific tranche around our recent historic average, licensed administration, low out-of-quota rate, short duration with mandatory review, and enforcement text that doesn't become a backdoor restriction. No concessions were made or implied by us. No numbers were put down by either side. This is consistent with holding firm in round one to test how much movement the June deadline forces out of them before we reveal any flexibility.

instruction: Hold the line again this round, but shift from pure rejection to constructive pressure. Restate that a global FCFS TRQ is unacceptable and reiterate the ask for a country-specific tranche reflecting our historic trade share, licensed administration, and preservation of TCA preference. Do not name a floor figure or a percentage yet. Instead, press the EU to respond concretely to our allocation-method question from round 1 — ask them directly how they intend to reflect 'principal supplying interest' in the design, not just acknowledge it procedurally. Use their June Council deadline explicitly: note that the UK is prepared to negotiate at pace, but only on a basis that takes country-specific allocation as the starting architecture, not first-come-first-served with a UK carve-out bolted on as a concession. On TCA disapplication, maintain that this is not a minor drafting matter and signal it sits outside the ordinary trade space for this negotiation — do not concede an inch on it this round, but don't yet declare it permanently non-negotiable either; leave it as 'a fundamental problem for the UK' without foreclosing later movement. You may indicate, without commitment, that the UK is open to discussing enforcement/anti-circumvention text and a review clause as areas where early technical progress could build confidence — this costs us nothing and tests their good faith. Do not engage on compensation elsewhere in their schedule yet; tell them we will address compensation once the TRQ architecture question (global vs country-specific) is resolved in principle, since compensation should offset agreed damage, not be negotiated against an undefined baseline.

public_message: Thank you for the clarity on your opening position. On allocation method, the Commission's institutional starting point remains a global pool administered on a non-discriminatory basis; that is a matter of legal design consistency across our schedule, not a judgement on the UK's trade share specifically. We would note that a global pool does not exclude UK access commensurate with your actual trade performance, and we're not persuaded that a global quota is inherently structured against any single supplier. That said, we are not closing the door on how the mechanics work in practice. As a sign of good faith, and independent of your specific ask, we are prepared to table a shorter duration than an open-ended measure — in the order of three years — with a mandatory review clause, reflecting our own view that the overcapacity picture may evolve and that a fixed re-examination point is sensible regardless of this negotiation. On enforcement and anti-circumvention, we are willing to look at drafting that addresses genuine transhipment risk without functioning as a disguised restriction on legitimately UK-origin product — that's a technical exercise we can scope together, separate from the FTA/TCA disapplication question, which remains part of the general measure for all non-EEA partners. On TCA disapplication itself, we are not in a position to offer a carve-out at this stage. Before we discuss allocation mechanics further, we would find it useful to understand what the UK is prepared to put on the table by way of compensation elsewhere in our schedule — and whether your 'historic average' figure is your substantive floor or an opening position, since that will shape how productive further discussion of volume and method can be.

public_message: We note the movement on duration and a mandatory review clause — a three-year term with built-in re-examination is compatible with our own position, and we're content to record that as a shared building block, without prejudice to the rest of the package. We also welcome your willingness to scope anti-circumvention drafting as a technical track; we can begin that work in parallel. But let's be precise about where we actually are: you have not moved on the core architecture. Restating that a global pool is 'non-discriminatory' does not answer our point — a first-come first-served global quota systematically disadvantages a supplier like the UK, with a narrower product range and shorter shipping distance dynamics than larger volume suppliers, regardless of our 'actual trade performance', because performance under FCFS is a function of allocation mechanics, not underlying trade share. That is precisely why Article XXVIII asks you to have regard to principal supplying interest in the design, not merely to consult us procedurally and then apply a formula that ignores it. We'd ask directly: what allocation mechanism does the Commission propose that actually reflects UK trade share, if not a country-specific tranche? If the answer is 'none', say so plainly, because that changes what we're negotiating. On TCA disapplication, we're not going to treat 'it remains part of the general measure' as a closed matter — the UK is a bilateral FTA partner with specific obligations negotiated under the TCA, not a third country caught incidentally in an anti-overcapacity measure aimed at non-market economies, and unwinding that inside this process has consequences beyond this file. We are not asking you to reopen the TCA; we are asking you not to use this measure to do it by the back door. On compensation: we're not going to negotiate compensation against an undefined injury. Once we have clarity on allocation architecture — specifically, whether you're prepared to move to a country-specific share — we can discuss compensation in the round, as part of a single package. Until then we'd be negotiating against ourselves.

report: Round 2 held. The UK accepted our tabled three-year duration with mandatory review as a 'shared building block' and agreed to scope anti-circumvention/transhipment drafting as a parallel technical track — both without prejudice to the rest of the package. That is real, if modest, progress and costs us nothing structurally. However, the UK pushed hard on the core architecture: they rejected our line that a global FCFS pool is compatible with 'principal supplying interest' recognition, arguing performance under FCFS is a function of allocation mechanics rather than trade share, and asked us directly whether we are proposing any mechanism that reflects UK share if not a country-specific tranche. They did not move off their opening ask (tranche near their historic ~2.4Mt average, licensed administration). On TCA disapplication, they again refused to treat it as settled, framing it as a bilateral-obligation issue distinct from the NME-overcapacity rationale, and explicitly flagged 'consequences beyond this file' — consistent with our intelligence on Japan/Korea encouraging a joint FTA response. Most significantly, the UK is now declining to discuss compensation at all until we clarify whether we will move to a country-specific share, explicitly refusing to 'negotiate against themselves.' This is a deliberate sequencing tactic to extract a structural concession before disclosing their compensation offer.

recommendation.reasoning: We should not break the compensation deadlock by moving on allocation architecture yet — that is exactly the sequencing the UK is trying to impose, and doing so in round 2 would confirm that firmness is unnecessary and invite the same tactic from Turkey/Korea/Japan in their parallel processes. But we are now at a genuine impasse: the UK has said plainly it will not put a compensation offer on the table without some signal on allocation. We have banked duration/review and opened an enforcement track, which is useful but not sufficient to keep this process moving toward a June conclusion. I need capital's steer on whether we can float, in round 3, a fallback structural option short of a full country-specific tranche — e.g., a global pool with a guaranteed minimum access mechanism or licensed sub-window for principal suppliers, without naming a country-specific volume — as a way to test whether the UK's real objective is method (protection from FCFS disadvantage) or volume (a fixed share near 2.4Mt). This lets us probe their true floor while still not conceding a country-specific tranche outright. On TCA, the political risk of continued refusal is rising given the Japan/Korea coalition risk; I recommend authority to explore, at most, enforcement-based reassurance (not a carve-out) but flag that if the UK treats this as a walk-away issue, we may need Brussels-level political judgment on whether the wider systemic cost of a UK-Japan-Korea joint FTA action outweighs the value of holding this line.

instruction: Move to round 3 as follows. First, formally note for the record that duration (3 years) and a mandatory review clause are agreed building blocks, and that the anti-circumvention/transhipment drafting track is under way in parallel — banked, not reopened. Second, break the sequencing impasse by tabling, as an EU-initiated idea (not a response to their demand), the concept of a licensed 'principal supplier' sub-window operating inside the global 400,000t pool: a portion of the pool would be available for licensed drawdown by suppliers with demonstrated historic trade on these lines (this would in practice cover the UK, Turkey and Korea), with the remainder administered FCFS. Do not name a UK-specific tonnage or percentage, and do not concede that this is a country-specific allocation — frame it explicitly as a licensing mechanism operating within a still-global pool, addressing their stated objection to FCFS mechanics rather than conceding on volume or on 'principal supplying interest' being reflected in a fixed national share. Make clear this is a conditional offer: we expect the UK, within this same round, to (a) put a concrete compensation offer on the table covering rebalancing elsewhere in our schedule, and (b) clarify what treatment EU exporters can expect under the UK's own parallel steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process, since that is directly relevant to what 'substantially equivalent' compensation looks like in the round. If pressed for a number on the licensed window, do not give one — say the mechanics must be agreed in principle before shares are discussed, and that any figure depends on trade data still being finalised. Hold the line completely on TCA/FTA disapplication as a general feature of the measure for all non-EEA partners; you may offer, as a technical reassurance only, that the 3-year review clause could include an explicit re-examination point on how the measure interacts with FTA preference schedules generally — this is not a carve-out and must not be presented as one. Do not increase the total pool above 400,000 tonnes this round. Do not disclose any internal floor figures.

report: Second round held. EU tabled a modest but real concession: they are now prepared to accept a three-year duration with a mandatory review clause, and framed this as independent of the negotiation rather than a direct trade — but it aligns with our target and we recorded it as a shared building block without prejudice. They also offered to scope anti-circumvention/transhipment drafting as a parallel technical track, which costs us nothing to accept and may build some confidence. However, on the two issues that matter most — allocation architecture and TCA disapplication — the EU has not moved. They restated the global pool as a 'legal design consistency' matter and argued it isn't inherently discriminatory, without answering our direct question of what mechanism (if any) would reflect UK principal supplying interest in the allocation method itself. On TCA disapplication, they explicitly said they are 'not in a position to offer a carve-out at this stage' and are holding it as part of the general measure for all non-EEA partners. They also pressed us twice now: once for our view of substantially equivalent compensation, and now more pointedly for whether our historic-average figure is a floor or an opening position, and for compensation elsewhere in their schedule — clearly trying to get us to move first on substance while they've only moved on process/duration. We held firm: we did not name a tranche figure, did not concede TCA disapplication as negotiable, and declined to discuss compensation until allocation architecture is clarified, framing it correctly as a single package. We did directly force the question of whether 'no country-specific mechanism at all' is their real answer — worth watching how they respond next round, since if they concede nothing there we have grounds to characterise this as non-compliant with Article XXVIII's principal-supplying-interest requirement in Geneva committee terms, which has broader reputational value even if it doesn't change their calculus alone.

public_message: Let's record where we've landed before moving forward. Duration of three years with a mandatory review clause, and the anti-circumvention/transhipment drafting track, are agreed building blocks — banked, not reopened. On the core architecture, we have listened carefully to your objection that FCFS mechanics, not trade share, determine outcomes under a global pool, and we want to test whether that is genuinely your concern rather than a fixed volume demand. We are prepared to explore, as an EU-initiated concept, a licensed 'principal supplier' sub-window operating inside the global 400,000-tonne pool: a portion of the pool available for licensed drawdown by suppliers with demonstrated historic trade on these lines, with the remainder administered first-come first-served. To be precise: this is a licensing mechanism within a still-global pool, not a country-specific allocation, and we are not in a position today to name a UK-specific tonnage or percentage — the mechanics need to be agreed in principle, and any figures depend on trade data still being finalised. We think this is a substantive response to the objection you raised, and we'd now expect movement from you in the same round: first, a concrete compensation offer covering rebalancing elsewhere in our schedule; and second, clarity on what treatment EU exporters can expect under the UK's own parallel steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process, since that bears directly on what substantially equivalent compensation looks like. On TCA/FTA disapplication, it remains a general feature of the measure applying to all non-EEA partners — we are not offering a carve-out. What we can offer is that the three-year review clause include an explicit re-examination point on how the measure interacts with FTA preference schedules generally, across all affected partners. That is a technical reassurance on process, not a substantive exemption, and should not be read as one.

public_message: We record the three-year duration, mandatory review clause and the anti-circumvention technical track as agreed building blocks, and thank you for the FTA-interaction re-examination point in the review clause — that is welcome as a process safeguard, but let's be clear: it is not a substantive answer to our TCA concern, and we do not accept it as such. On the principal-supplier sub-window: this is the first substantive move on architecture and we're prepared to engage with it seriously, but as tabled it doesn't yet meet the Article XXVIII test. A licensing sub-window inside a 400,000-tonne global pool only matters if we know its size relative to the whole, its eligibility criteria, and whether it guarantees UK access commensurate with our historic share rather than simply competing UK licence-holders against other principal suppliers for a slice of an already inadequate pool. Two things follow. First, the 400,000-tonne total pool itself is a live question, not a fixed backdrop — a sub-window carved from a pool that is roughly one-sixth of current UK trade alone does not solve the underlying volume problem, and we'd expect the pool to be sized with that in mind. Second, on sizing the sub-window: as an indicative anchor, not a floor, we're looking at a guaranteed share in the region of 70 to 85 percent of our recent historic average trade on these lines being available to the UK specifically within whatever mechanism you design — whether that's delivered as a country-specific tranche or a sub-window with a UK-specific minimum guaranteed drawdown is a technical question we can work through, provided the effect is equivalent. We need a concrete figure from you on sub-window size and eligibility before we can assess whether this converges with that anchor. On compensation: once we see that figure, we can move to compensation in the same round — we're not stalling, we're sequencing correctly, since compensation has to offset a defined injury. On your question about EU exporters under the UK's own measure: that is a parallel process and we're not pre-negotiating its outcome here, but we note that reciprocal treatment there is itself part of the substantially equivalent value question, and we're content to discuss it as part of a single package once your side has put a real number on the table for the sub-window.

report: Round 3 closed with the UK banking the same building blocks (3-year duration, mandatory review clause, anti-circumvention track) and explicitly declining to treat our FTA-interaction re-examination point as a substantive answer on TCA/FTA disapplication — they logged it as 'welcome but not sufficient.' On architecture, the UK engaged seriously with the licensed principal-supplier sub-window concept for the first time but immediately reopened the total pool size as 'a live question, not a fixed backdrop,' arguing 400,000t is structurally inadequate given their ~2.4Mt trade. They then tabled an explicit anchor: a guaranteed UK share of 70-85% of their historic average (roughly 1.68-2.04Mt), whether delivered as a country-specific tranche or a sub-window with a UK-specific minimum guarantee — they say the vehicle is a technical question provided the effect is equivalent. This anchor is far outside anything in our current mandate; it exceeds our internal calibration ceiling (approx. 15-18% of the 400,000t pool, i.e. 60,000-72,000t) by a factor of roughly 25-30x, and would itself exceed the entire notified pool several times over. The UK continues to withhold both a compensation offer and clarity on EU exporters' treatment under their own parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII process, now explicitly conditioning both on us naming a concrete sub-window figure first. This is the same sequencing tactic as round 2, but escalated — they've moved from refusing to negotiate 'against an undefined injury' to anchoring a number that makes clear the gap between us is not just about mechanics but about volume itself, and it is very large.

recommendation.reasoning: We should not move toward the UK's anchor, which is wildly out of proportion to our mandate and to what a 'substantially equivalent' remedy under Article XXVIII plausibly requires — it would gut the measure's purpose. report: Round 3 held. The EU tabled its first substantive architecture move: a licensed 'principal supplier' sub-window inside the still-global 400,000t pool, with a portion reserved for licensed drawdown by historic suppliers and the remainder FCFS. They also offered a review-clause addition: an explicit re-examination point on FTA/TCA interaction generally across affected partners — but held firm that TCA disapplication itself remains part of the general measure, no carve-out. Duration (3 years), mandatory review, and the anti-circumvention technical track remain banked as agreed building blocks from round 2, reaffirmed by both sides. The EU pressed hard for two things in return: a concrete UK compensation offer on their schedule, and clarity on EU exporter treatment under the UK's own parallel safeguard/Art XXVIII process, arguing the latter bears on 'substantially equivalent value'. We did not concede either. We welcomed the sub-window concept as the first real architecture movement but declined to assess it without a concrete size/eligibility figure from them, restated our 70-85% historic-share anchor (already floated last round) as the test for convergence, and explicitly kept the 400,000t total pool itself as a live/contestable number rather than a fixed backdrop — pushing back on the idea that a sub-window carved from an inadequate total solves anything. We declined to name compensation or engage on the UK's own measure until the EU puts a real number on the sub-window, framing this as correct sequencing rather than stalling. We did not disclose our 2.0m tonne floor, our 20% out-of-quota ceiling, or any absolute tonnage. TCA disapplication remains unresolved and unescalated — held as a serious structural problem without declaring it a permanent red line, consistent with London's steer.

instruction: This is the final round — treat it as such. Structure: (1) Recap and lock in what's banked: 3-year duration, mandatory review clause, anti-circumvention technical track. State these are contingent on overall settlement, not free-standing. (2) Force the architecture question to a close. Tell the EU plainly: a licensing sub-window carved out of a 400,000-tonne total pool cannot mathematically deliver a UK-specific outcome anywhere near our historic trade share, because our own trade alone (2.4m tonnes) is six times the entire proposed pool. Say explicitly that the total pool size is therefore not a side issue — it is the whole issue — and ask them, in terms, whether the Commission is prepared to increase the total pool to a level that can actually accommodate a UK guarantee of the scale we've flagged, or whether they are conceding that the sub-window is cosmetic. (3) Table our real number, for the first time, as our position for closing today: a guaranteed UK-specific tranche or equivalent minimum drawdown right of approximately 1.8–2.0 million tonnes annually (roughly 75–83% of our recent average), with an out-of-quota rate no higher than 20%, on the agreed 3-year duration with mandatory review. Frame this explicitly as 'what would let us recommend settlement to ministers this round' — not an opening bid. (4) Table concrete compensation for the first time: the UK is prepared to improve country-specific quota allocations for EU exporters under our own parallel steel safeguard measure, calibrated to reflect a fair reciprocal share, conditional on the EU meeting the volume/rate package above. Make clear this has real value given the EU's own significant exposure to our safeguard. (5) On TCA/FTA disapplication: signal, for the first time, that the UK could accept the general disapplication applying to UK-origin steel under this measure specifically and only if the full package above (tranche ~1.8–2.0m tonnes, out-of-quota rate ≤20%, 3yr+review) is agreed in full, AND the review clause names TCA interaction specifically as a mandatory item for re-examination at an 18-month interim point, not merely a generic FTA reference. Do not concede this unconditionally, and do not concede it at all if the volume/rate package falls materially short. (6) Be explicit that this is the UK's final position for this process: if the EU cannot move to something close to this today, say clearly that the UK does not believe a negotiated outcome is achievable within the timeline, and that the UK will treat the process as concluded without agreement, reserving all rights under Article XXVIII including withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, and noting that other affected principal suppliers are watching how this is resolved. Do not go further than this without checking back — if the EU offers something materially close but not identical (e.g. 1.6m tonnes at 22% out-of-quota), hold the line at the table, note it as insufficient, and refer it back rather than agreeing on the spot.

authority.notes: This is the genuine bottom line for this final round, not a public opening figure. Absolute floor for closing today: tranche/guaranteed drawdown no lower than 1.5 million tonnes (62% of historic average) AND out-of-quota rate no higher than 25% AND 3yr duration with binding review AND EU commitment to increase total pool materially beyond 400,000t to accommodate this without simply cannibalising other claimants' shares. TCA/FTA disapplication may be accepted ONLY if the full package (tranche ≥1.5m, rate ≤25%, review with named TCA re-examination point) is met — if the EU offers less than this combination, do not concede TCA under any circumstances. If the EU's offer falls short of the absolute floor on volume and rate together, do not settle — accept the no-agreement outcome and preserve withdrawal rights rather than lock in a bad permanent architecture. Compensation offer (UK safeguard quota improvement for EU exporters) is conditional and should only be confirmed as agreed if the EU meets at least the floor package.

public_message: We come to this round prepared to name a concrete figure, as we said we would. This is not a country-specific UK allocation, and it does not come with a guarantee tied to your historic average; it is a licensing mechanism addressing the FCFS-mechanics objection you raised, sized at what we consider defensible within a measure whose total volume and 50% out-of-quota rate are not open questions. Duration of three years, the mandatory review clause including the FTA-interaction re-examination point, and the anti-circumvention track remain as agreed building blocks. public_message: We appreciate you naming a figure, but let's be precise about what it actually is. A 72,000-tonne sub-window, shared between the UK, Turkey and Korea, inside a 400,000-tonne pool that itself remains unchanged, against UK trade of 2.4 million tonnes, is not a response to the principal-supplying-interest objection we have raised since round one — it is a rounding error against it. It does not meet the Article XXVIII standard, and it does not come close to anything the UK can present to ministers as substantially equivalent treatment. We had indicated, as our position for closing this process, a guaranteed UK drawdown in the region of 1.8–2.0 million tonnes, an out-of-quota rate no higher than 20%, and a total pool sized to accommodate that without simply cannibalising other claimants' shares. You have told us the 50% out-of-quota rate and the 400,000-tonne total are not open questions, and that your sub-window figure is final. On that basis there is no package on the table that bears any relationship to our floor, and we are not willing to close this at the level you've described. We are not in a position to table compensation on our schedule, or to give clarity on treatment of EU exporters under our own safeguard measure, against a core offer of this scale — compensation has to offset a defined injury, and 72,000 tonnes shared three ways does not define one we can accept. We will record that the UK regards the notified measure, absent the movement we've set out, as inconsistent with the regard due to a principal supplying interest under Article XXVIII. If the EU proceeds with the measure as notified, the UK will consider its position on withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, as provided for under Article XXVIII, and will do so on a timeline that reflects the scale of what has just been proposed. We record the three-year duration, mandatory review clause with FTA-interaction re-examination, and the anti-circumvention technical track as items we were prepared to conclude as part of a genuine package — that offer lapses along with the rest if there is no wider settlement. This process closes today without agreement on our side. We remain open to resuming discussion before the measure takes legal effect if the Commission is able to return with a materially different figure on total volume, UK-specific access, and out-of-quota rate — but we are not going to pretend that what has been tabled today is close enough to hold this open on our current terms.

report: Round 4, the final round, closed without settlement. This was explicitly presented as final, not an opening bid, and conditioned on the UK reciprocating with a concrete compensation offer and clarity on EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII measure. The UK rejected this outright as 'a rounding error' against their principal-supplying interest, restated their closing position as a guaranteed UK drawdown of 1.8–2.0 million tonnes, an out-of-quota rate no higher than 20%, and a total pool resized to accommodate that without cannibalising other claimants. They declined to table compensation or safeguard-reciprocity clarity against our offer, stated they are not willing to close on our terms, and formally closed the process on their side without agreement — while noting for the record that the previously agreed building blocks (duration, review clause, anti-circumvention track) lapse along with the rest absent a wider settlement. They flagged that the UK will consider withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions under Article XXVIII if the EU proceeds as notified, 'on a timeline that reflects the scale' of today's offer — a signal of intent to escalate rather than an immediate declaration. report: Round 4 concluded without agreement. The EU tabled what it called a final, non-improvable offer: a 72,000-tonne licensed 'principal supplier' sub-window inside the unchanged 400,000-tonne global pool, shared on equal eligibility terms between the UK, Turkey and Korea — no UK-specific guarantee, no increase to the total pool, and the 50% out-of-quota rate confirmed as fixed and non-negotiable. They demanded a concrete UK compensation offer and clarity on EU exporter treatment under our own safeguard measure as the price of keeping the process open today. I declined to table compensation or safeguard-treatment clarity against an offer of this scale, stated plainly that 72,000 tonnes split three ways does not meet the Article XXVIII principal-supplying-interest standard against our 2.4m tonnes of trade, and closed the process on our side without agreement, while preserving the previously-discussed duration/review/anti-circumvention items as having lapsed with the rest of the package. I put down a formal marker that the UK regards the notified measure as inconsistent with the regard due to a principal supplying interest, and flagged that the UK will consider withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions if the EU proceeds as notified.
